titleStmt.title: Flourishing Across Europe: Application of a New Conceptual Framework for Defining Well-Being
titleStmt.author: Felicia A. Huppert
Timothy T. C. So

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Flourishing Across Europe: Application of a New Conceptual Framework for Defining Well-Being

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A DEFINITION BUILT BY NEGATING ANOTHER DEFINITION - the symptoms of depression and generalised anxiety in DSM-IV and ICD-10, inverted one at a time by a panel of four, to give ten features of positive well-being
span.quote: A conceptual framework is offered which equates high well-being with positive mental health. Well-being is seen as lying at the opposite end of a spectrum to the common mental disorders (depression, anxiety). By examining internationally agreed criteria for depression and anxiety (DSM and ICD classifications), and defining the opposite of each symptom, we identify ten features of positive well-being. These combine feeling and functioning, i.e. hedonic and eudaimonic aspects of well-being: competence, emotional stability, engagement, meaning, optimism, positive emotion, positive relationships, resilience, self esteem, and vitality.

span.label: how well-being should be measured, given that a dozen conceptual definitions exist with no agreement on which to use, and that surveys routinely substitute a single life-satisfaction item for all of them
span.quote: The dedicated study of flourishing requires an accepted definition and good quality scales by which to measure it. Although various definitions and scales exist, deriving from a variety of theoretical and empirical perspectives (see below), there is no current agreement on which should be used in research, or to inform policy. In the same way that it has taken many years for clinicians to agree on the diagnosis of mental disorders (and this remains a dynamic process as our understanding of mental disorders increases), it will take some years to achieve agreement on the definition and measurement of mental health.

span.label: ten features of flourishing deduced from the diagnostic criteria for the common mental disorders, an operational definition combining them in the shape DSM uses for a diagnosis, and its application to 43,000 people in 23 countries
span.quote: Following this approach, we proposed that positive emotion be a required feature, given that it is the only feature which addresses the hedonic (emotional) aspect of well-being. We also proposed that the majority of the symptoms in each of the ‘positive characteristics’ and ‘positive functioning’ factors be present. The criterion we selected was having all but one of the features of positive characteristics and all but one of the features of positive functioning, together with positive emotion. This was met by 15.8% of the total European sample, and adopted as our operational definition of flourishing.

span.label: a positive construct with no agreed definition, in a field that had been measuring it with one question
span.quote: This illustrative, though far from complete, list of approaches to conceptualising well-being serves to indicate both the overlaps and the differences between existing definitions. The one thing they all have in common is the view that well-being is multi-dimensional. This contrasts sharply with the long-standing assumption, made in generations of economic and social surveys, that positive human experience can be adequately assessed using a single item about life satisfaction or happiness.

span.label: deduction from two diagnostic classifications by a panel of three psychologists and one lay person, then psychometric analysis (Spearman correlations, exploratory factor analysis, multi-group CFA for measurement equivalence) on European Social Survey Round 3 data
span.term: deduction from two diagnostic classifications by a panel of three psychologists and one lay person, then psychometric analysis (Spearman correlations, exploratory factor analysis, multi-group CFA for measurement equivalence) on European Social Survey Round 3 data
span.quote: In order to identify the mirror opposite of the symptoms of generalised anxiety and depression, a panel of four individuals (three psychologists and one lay person) began by expressing in simple English the words or phrases which best seemed to capture the positive pole of each symptom. Somatic symptoms, such as significant weight loss, sleep problems or psychomotor agitation, were not included, mainly because our focus was on mental states rather than physical states. Also, it is not clear what the positive pole of these physical symptoms would be. We then assigned a single word or pair of words which in our judgement best summarised each positive concept.

span.label: **A DEFINITION BUILT BY NEGATING ANOTHER DEFINITION, SYMPTOM BY SYMPTOM**: `By examining INTERNATIONALLY AGREED CRITERIA FOR DEPRESSION AND ANXIETY (DSM AND ICD CLASSIFICATIONS), and DEFINING THE OPPOSITE OF EACH SYMPTOM, we identify TEN FEATURES of positive well-being.` The corpus holds vocabularies revised, voted, counted and reclassified; this is one DERIVED FROM ANOTHER by inversion, and the derivation is the method section
span.quote: A conceptual framework is offered which equates high well-being with positive mental health. Well-being is seen as lying at the opposite end of a spectrum to the common mental disorders (depression, anxiety). By examining internationally agreed criteria for depression and anxiety (DSM and ICD classifications), and defining the opposite of each symptom, we identify ten features of positive well-being. These combine feeling and functioning, i.e. hedonic and eudaimonic aspects of well-being: competence, emotional stability, engagement, meaning, optimism, positive emotion, positive relationships, resilience, self esteem, and vitality.

span.label: **AND IT INHERITS THE SOURCE'S BLIND SPOTS, WHICH THE AUTHORS PRINT**: `AUTONOMY WAS NOT INCLUDED IN OUR LIST OF FEATURES BECAUSE ITS OPPOSITE IS NOT SPECIFIED IN DSM OR ICD DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA for depression or anxiety. That is, LOSS OF AUTONOMY IS NOT REGARDED AS A SYMPTOM of these disorders. THIS RAISES THE QUESTION ABOUT THE NECESSITY OF AUTONOMY AS AN ELEMENT IN POSITIVE HUMAN FUNCTIONING.` A concept central to Jahoda, Ryff, and Ryan & Deci is absent for NO REASON EXCEPT THE SHAPE OF THE SOURCE VOCABULARY - and the authors turn the absence into a question about the world rather than about their method
span.quote: However, what the ten features do not include is psychodynamic constructs such as ‘personal growth’ or ‘self acceptance’ (Ryff 1989 ), or the construct of autonomy or self-determination, which is a central concept for Jahoda ( 1958 ), Ryan and Deci ( 2001 ), Ryff ( 1989 ), and Ryff and Keyes ( 1995 ). Autonomy was not included in our list of features because its opposite is not specified in DSM or ICD diagnostic criteria for depression or anxiety. That is, loss of autonomy is not regarded as a symptom of these disorders. This raises the question about the necessity of autonomy as an element in positive human functioning. Outside the clinical context, some cross-cultural researchers have suggested that while autonomy may be regarded as important for well-being in Western nations, it is less relevant in collectivist countries such as many in Asia and Africa

span.label: AND A WHOLE CLASS IS EXCLUDED BECAUSE THE NEGATION IS UNDEFINED: `the other categories of anxiety disorder (phobias, OCD, PTSD) DO NOT HAVE A POLAR OPPOSITE. For example, one either has a phobia (of different levels of severity) or not, but IT IS DIFFICULT TO SEE WHAT THE POSITIVE POLE OF A DISTRIBUTION OF PHOBIA COULD BE.` The method can only reach the disorders whose symptoms sit on a continuum with a positive end - and somatic symptoms go the same way, `it is NOT CLEAR WHAT THE POSITIVE POLE OF THESE PHYSICAL SYMPTOMS WOULD BE`
span.quote: The second reason is that the other categories of anxiety disorder (phobias, OCD, PTSD) do not have a polar opposite. For example, one either has a phobia (of different levels of severity) or not, but it is difficult to see what the positive pole of a distribution of phobia could be. The same applies to OCD and PTSD. In contrast, for depression and generalised anxiety, one can go beyond the neutral point where the symptoms are absent, to a positive pole, which represents such features as happiness and hopefulness (depression) or calmness and resilience (generalised anxiety).

span.label: AND THE INVERSION WAS DONE BY FOUR PEOPLE IN PLAIN ENGLISH: `a panel of four individuals (THREE PSYCHOLOGISTS AND ONE LAY PERSON) began by EXPRESSING IN SIMPLE ENGLISH the words or phrases which best seemed to CAPTURE THE POSITIVE POLE OF EACH SYMPTOM. ... We then assigned A SINGLE WORD OR PAIR OF WORDS WHICH IN OUR JUDGEMENT BEST SUMMARISED each positive concept.` And the honesty that follows: `SOME OPPOSITES WERE EASIER TO IDENTIFY WITH CONFIDENCE THAN OTHERS`
span.quote: In order to identify the mirror opposite of the symptoms of generalised anxiety and depression, a panel of four individuals (three psychologists and one lay person) began by expressing in simple English the words or phrases which best seemed to capture the positive pole of each symptom. Somatic symptoms, such as significant weight loss, sleep problems or psychomotor agitation, were not included, mainly because our focus was on mental states rather than physical states. Also, it is not clear what the positive pole of these physical symptoms would be. We then assigned a single word or pair of words which in our judgement best summarised each positive concept.

span.label: **AND THE THRESHOLD MOVED BECAUSE THE DATA WAS SKEWED**: `on two of the items, the responses were SO SKEWED that the vast majority of participants said they agreed (ENGAGEMENT 80.5%; POSITIVE RELATIONSHIPS 90.2%), SO IN THESE TWO CASES, WE USED THE `STRONGLY AGREE` CATEGORY ... We also calculated mean scores and found that for each item, THE CHOSEN CUT POINTS CORRESPONDED TO THE CATEGORY ABOVE THE MEAN.` The class boundary set by the response distribution, then checked against the mean afterwards
span.quote: Categorising a feature as present or absent required choosing an appropriate cut point, and this was largely determined by the type of response scale used. In the case of the seven items using the agree/disagree format, respondents were required to indicate that they agreed. However, on two of the items, the responses were so skewed that the vast majority of participants said they agreed (engagement 80.5%; positive relationships 90.2%), so in these two cases, we used the ‘strongly agree’ category. The positive emotion item also showed a very strong positive skew (median was between 7 and 8 on the 0–10 scale) so we chose 8–10 as our positive category. For the items about emotional stability and vitality, participants were categorised as demonstrating these characteristics if they responded ‘all or almost all of the time’ or ‘most of the time’. We also calculated mean scores and found that for each item, the chosen cut points corresponded to the category above the mean.

span.label: AND THE OPERATIONAL DEFINITION COPIES DSM'S SHAPE, NOT ONLY ITS CONTENT: `Diagnostic criteria for depression and anxiety DO NOT REQUIRE THAT ALL SYMPTOMS BE PRESENT. They do, however, require THE PRESENCE OF ONE OR TWO KEY SYMPTOMS ... Following this approach, we proposed that POSITIVE EMOTION BE A REQUIRED FEATURE ... The criterion we selected was having ALL BUT ONE of the features of positive characteristics and ALL BUT ONE of the features of positive functioning, together with positive emotion. THIS WAS MET BY 15.8% OF THE TOTAL EUROPEAN SAMPLE.` A required item plus a majority rule, borrowed from the classification being inverted
span.quote: Following this approach, we proposed that positive emotion be a required feature, given that it is the only feature which addresses the hedonic (emotional) aspect of well-being. We also proposed that the majority of the symptoms in each of the ‘positive characteristics’ and ‘positive functioning’ factors be present. The criterion we selected was having all but one of the features of positive characteristics and all but one of the features of positive functioning, together with positive emotion. This was met by 15.8% of the total European sample, and adopted as our operational definition of flourishing.

span.label: AND THE SOURCE VOCABULARY IS SAID TO HAVE BEEN OPINION: `before the advent of DSM-IV, DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA WERE BASED MORE ON THE PERSONAL OPINIONS OF MEMBERS OF THE DSM TASK FORCE THAN ON SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE. DSM-IV improved on this situation through the use of systematic evidence to support their decisions.` The paper cites that history as the reason it seeks data rather than deduction for the COMBINING step
span.quote: For instance, before the advent of DSM-IV, diagnostic criteria were based more on the personal opinions of members of the DSM task force than on scientific evidence. DSM-IV improved on this situation through the use of systematic evidence to support their decisions (Widiger and Clark 2000 ). Likewise, in order to decide how to combine features for the definition of flourishing, we sought data from a large, representative population sample to establish how the features are distributed in the population, and how they cluster together.

span.label: AND A DIAGNOSIS IS AN ARBITRARY CUT POINT, SAID PLAINLY: `It has been recognised for some time that A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS SUCH AS DEPRESSION REPRESENTS AN ARBITRARY CUT POINT ALONG A CONTINUUM. The cut point is intended to represent THE SEVERITY AT WHICH THE PERSON IS NO LONGER ABLE TO FUNCTION in their everyday life.` The source of the inversion is itself a threshold on a continuum, chosen for a practical consequence
span.quote: It has been recognised for some time (e.g. Anderson et al. 1993 ; Whittington and Huppert 1996 ) that a clinical diagnosis such as depression represents an arbitrary cut point along a continuum. The cut point is intended to represent the severity at which the person is no longer able to function in their everyday life.

span.label: AND A DOZEN CONCEPTUAL DEFINITIONS ALREADY EXISTED, OVERLAPPING AND DISAGREEING: `This illustrative, though far from complete, list of approaches to conceptualising well-being serves to indicate BOTH THE OVERLAPS AND THE DIFFERENCES BETWEEN EXISTING DEFINITIONS. THE ONE THING THEY ALL HAVE IN COMMON IS THE VIEW THAT WELL-BEING IS MULTI-DIMENSIONAL. This contrasts sharply with the long-standing assumption, made in GENERATIONS OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL SURVEYS, that positive human experience can be ADEQUATELY ASSESSED USING A SINGLE ITEM about life satisfaction or happiness.` Every theorist disagrees with every other, and all of them disagree with the surveys
span.quote: This illustrative, though far from complete, list of approaches to conceptualising well-being serves to indicate both the overlaps and the differences between existing definitions. The one thing they all have in common is the view that well-being is multi-dimensional. This contrasts sharply with the long-standing assumption, made in generations of economic and social surveys, that positive human experience can be adequately assessed using a single item about life satisfaction or happiness.

span.label: AND THEIR OWN EARLIER DEFINITION IS STILL IN CIRCULATION: `In an earlier briefing document which we prepared for an OECD meeting, WE USED AN OPERATIONAL DEFINITION WHICH FOCUSED ON DEPRESSION AS THE OPPOSITE OF FLOURISHING. THIS DOCUMENT WAS CITED BY SELIGMAN (2011) AND FORGEARD ET AL. (2011). The definition used in the present paper IS MORE COMPREHENSIVE, since it has considered the other common mental disorder, generalised anxiety, as well as depression.` Two versions of one team's definition, both cited, four years apart
span.quote: In an earlier briefing document which we prepared for an OECD meeting (Huppert and So 2009 ), we used an operational definition which focused on depression as the opposite of flourishing. This document was cited by Seligman ( 2011 ) and Forgeard et al. ( 2011 ). The definition used in the present paper is more comprehensive, since it has considered the other common mental disorder, generalised anxiety, as well as depression.

span.label: **THE AUTHORS PREDICT THE DIVERGENCE THEIR METHOD WILL PRODUCE**: `Subjective judgements were involved in THE SELECTION OF SURVEY ITEMS to be used as indicators of these features, as well as THE CUT-OFF SCORE ON EACH ITEM to establish whether it is present or absent, and THE NUMBER OF FEATURES REQUIRED to meet the criterion of flourishing. ... OTHER STUDIES WHICH USE DIFFERENT SURVEYS AND DIFFERENT ITEMS AS INDICATORS OF THE TEN FEATURES OF FLOURISHING MIGHT REACH A DIFFERENT CONCLUSION ABOUT CUT POINTS AND THE NUMBER AND COMBINATION OF FEATURES REQUIRED.` Three subjectivities enumerated, and the disagreement forecast in the paper that starts it
span.quote: While our definition of flourishing and the resulting ten features were derived in as objective a manner as possible, some elements of subjectivity were unavoidable. Subjective judgements were involved in the selection of survey items to be used as indicators of these features, as well as the cut-off score on each item to establish whether it is present or absent, and the number of features required to meet the criterion of flourishing. We selected items from the European Social Survey (Round 3), because of its size, representativeness and comprehensive coverage of well-being; we chose item cut points based chiefly on their response format, but also made an adjustment if responses were very skewed; and the operational definition was largely based on the factorial structure of the data. Other studies which use different surveys and different items as indicators of the ten features of flourishing might reach a different conclusion about cut points and the number and combination of features required.

span.label: AND THE OPERATIONALISATION IS BOUNDED BY WHAT A SURVEY HAPPENED TO ASK: `FIVE FEATURES of flourishing were represented BY ONLY A SINGLE ITEM (competence, emotional stability, meaning, optimism, resilience) ... From a psychometric perspective IT WOULD HAVE BEEN PREFERABLE TO HAVE SEVERAL GOOD ITEMS PER CONSTRUCT, BUT SUCH DATA WERE NOT AVAILABLE.` Half the construct rests on one question each, and the reason is availability - the same shape as the gout criteria's dispensing data and EWGSOP's missing reference populations
span.quote: Five features of flourishing were represented by only a single item (competence, emotional stability, meaning, optimism, resilience), so for the remaining five we decided to choose the item which seemed to best capture the construct. From a psychometric perspective it would have been preferable to have several good items per construct, but such data were not available.

span.label: AND THE MULTI-DIMENSIONAL MEASURE OVERLAPS THE SINGLE-ITEM ONE ONLY MODESTLY: `The Spearman correlation between flourishing and life satisfaction was .34 ... AROUND HALF of those who were flourishing had high life satisfaction, and AROUND ONE THIRD of those with high life satisfaction were flourishing. Clearly, flourishing and life satisfaction are OVERLAPPING BUT DISTINCT CONCEPTS, and A GREAT DEAL WOULD BE LOST by measuring life satisfaction alone, ALTHOUGH THERE IS FREQUENTLY PRESSURE IN LARGE SCALE SURVEYS TO DO SO.`
span.quote: When we examined the relationship between life satisfaction and flourishing, we found a correlation of .34. At the individual level, the overlap was modest; around half of those who were flourishing had high life satisfaction, and around one third of those with high life satisfaction were flourishing. Clearly, flourishing and life satisfaction are overlapping but distinct concepts, and a great deal would be lost by measuring life satisfaction alone, although there is frequently pressure in large scale surveys to do so.

span.label: and the country spread is fourfold: `Application of this definition to respondents from the 23 countries which participated in the European Social Survey (Round 3) reveals A FOUR-FOLD DIFFERENCE IN FLOURISHING RATE, FROM 41% IN DENMARK TO LESS THAN 10% IN SLOVAKIA, RUSSIA AND PORTUGAL` - against 15.8% for Europe as a whole under the same definition
span.quote: Application of this definition to respondents from the 23 countries which participated in the European Social Survey (Round 3) reveals a four-fold difference in flourishing rate, from 41% in Denmark to less than 10% in Slovakia, Russia and Portugal. There are also striking differences in country profiles across the 10 features. These profiles offer fresh insight into cultural differences in well-being, and indicate which features may provide the most promising targets for policies to improve well-being. Comparison with a life satisfaction measure shows that valuable information would be lost if well-being was measured by life satisfaction.

At the individual level, the overlap was modest; around half of those who were flourishing had high life satisfaction, and around one third of those with high life satisfaction were flourishing. Clearly, flourishing and life satisfaction are overlapping but distinct concepts, and a great deal would be lost by measuring life satisfaction alone, although there is frequently pressure in large scale surveys to do so.

span.quote: A conceptual framework is offered which equates high well-being with positive mental health. Well-being is seen as lying at the opposite end of a spectrum to the common mental disorders (depression, anxiety). By examining internationally agreed criteria for depression and anxiety (DSM and ICD classifications), and defining the opposite of each symptom, we identify ten features of positive well-being. These combine feeling and functioning, i.e. hedonic and eudaimonic aspects of well-being: competence, emotional stability, engagement, meaning, optimism, positive emotion, positive relationships, resilience, self esteem, and vitality.

span.quote: However, what the ten features do not include is psychodynamic constructs such as ‘personal growth’ or ‘self acceptance’ (Ryff 1989 ), or the construct of autonomy or self-determination, which is a central concept for Jahoda ( 1958 ), Ryan and Deci ( 2001 ), Ryff ( 1989 ), and Ryff and Keyes ( 1995 ). Autonomy was not included in our list of features because its opposite is not specified in DSM or ICD diagnostic criteria for depression or anxiety. That is, loss of autonomy is not regarded as a symptom of these disorders. This raises the question about the necessity of autonomy as an element in positive human functioning. Outside the clinical context, some cross-cultural researchers have suggested that while autonomy may be regarded as important for well-being in Western nations, it is less relevant in collectivist countries such as many in Asia and Africa

span.quote: Categorising a feature as present or absent required choosing an appropriate cut point, and this was largely determined by the type of response scale used. In the case of the seven items using the agree/disagree format, respondents were required to indicate that they agreed. However, on two of the items, the responses were so skewed that the vast majority of participants said they agreed (engagement 80.5%; positive relationships 90.2%), so in these two cases, we used the ‘strongly agree’ category. The positive emotion item also showed a very strong positive skew (median was between 7 and 8 on the 0–10 scale) so we chose 8–10 as our positive category. For the items about emotional stability and vitality, participants were categorised as demonstrating these characteristics if they responded ‘all or almost all of the time’ or ‘most of the time’. We also calculated mean scores and found that for each item, the chosen cut points corresponded to the category above the mean.

span.quote: While our definition of flourishing and the resulting ten features were derived in as objective a manner as possible, some elements of subjectivity were unavoidable. Subjective judgements were involved in the selection of survey items to be used as indicators of these features, as well as the cut-off score on each item to establish whether it is present or absent, and the number of features required to meet the criterion of flourishing. We selected items from the European Social Survey (Round 3), because of its size, representativeness and comprehensive coverage of well-being; we chose item cut points based chiefly on their response format, but also made an adjustment if responses were very skewed; and the operational definition was largely based on the factorial structure of the data. Other studies which use different surveys and different items as indicators of the ten features of flourishing might reach a different conclusion about cut points and the number and combination of features required.

span.quote: For instance, before the advent of DSM-IV, diagnostic criteria were based more on the personal opinions of members of the DSM task force than on scientific evidence. DSM-IV improved on this situation through the use of systematic evidence to support their decisions (Widiger and Clark 2000 ). Likewise, in order to decide how to combine features for the definition of flourishing, we sought data from a large, representative population sample to establish how the features are distributed in the population, and how they cluster together.

span.label: `POSITIVE EMOTION as a required feature, together with ALL BUT ONE of the features of positive characteristics and ALL BUT ONE of the features of positive functioning` - met by 15.8% of the European sample
span.quote: Following this approach, we proposed that positive emotion be a required feature, given that it is the only feature which addresses the hedonic (emotional) aspect of well-being. We also proposed that the majority of the symptoms in each of the ‘positive characteristics’ and ‘positive functioning’ factors be present. The criterion we selected was having all but one of the features of positive characteristics and all but one of the features of positive functioning, together with positive emotion. This was met by 15.8% of the total European sample, and adopted as our operational definition of flourishing.

span.label: `a FOUR-FOLD DIFFERENCE IN FLOURISHING RATE` across 23 countries under ONE definition
span.quote: Application of this definition to respondents from the 23 countries which participated in the European Social Survey (Round 3) reveals a four-fold difference in flourishing rate, from 41% in Denmark to less than 10% in Slovakia, Russia and Portugal. There are also striking differences in country profiles across the 10 features. These profiles offer fresh insight into cultural differences in well-being, and indicate which features may provide the most promising targets for policies to improve well-being. Comparison with a life satisfaction measure shows that valuable information would be lost if well-being was measured by life satisfaction.
